projects.title: Kanz
projects.summary: Kanz is a mobile financial platform designed to make everyday money movement simpler, giving users easier access to their salary, transfers, withdrawals, and card payments in one place.
projects.briefLead: They needed a mobile experience that could bring essential financial services together while making everyday actions such as accessing salary, transferring money, withdrawing funds, and managing cards feel simple and accessible.
projects.problemLead: Everyday financial tasks can become unnecessarily complicated when users need to move between different services, processes, and payment methods.
projects.approachLead: Designed Kanz around immediate access and control, bringing salary streaming, transfers, withdrawals, payments, and account management into one consistent mobile system.
projects.approachBody:
The experience is structured around the actions users perform most frequently.

Kanz creates one mobile hub for everyday financial activity, allowing users to access earned salary, transfer money instantly, withdraw funds, manage cards, and control account settings from one place. Task-focused flows keep important actions simple while maintaining visibility and security.
projects.shippedHeading: A financial experience built around access and control.
projects.reflectionLead: The goal was not simply to add more financial features, but to make access to money feel immediate, understandable, and under the user's control.
projects.reflectionBody: Kanz connects the most important financial actions into one mobile journey.

constraints.title: Salary access, transfers, withdrawals, and cards were treated as separate experiences.
Essential money movements involved multiple steps and could create unnecessary friction.
Users had limited flexibility over when and how they accessed their earned money.

decisions.title: Faster Access
decisions.body: Users can access earned salary without relying solely on traditional payday cycles.

decisions.title: Everyday Flexibility
decisions.body: Transfers, withdrawals, and payments are connected through one experience.

decisions.title: Greater Control
decisions.body: Account, card, notification, and security settings are managed in one place.

metrics.label: Access salary already earned before the regular payday.
A streamlined flow for selecting recipients, entering amounts, and sending money.
Flexible withdrawal methods and virtual card management for everyday spending.

seo.metaDescription: Kanz is a mobile financial platform designed to make everyday money movement simpler, giving users easier access to their salary, transfers, withdrawals, and card payments in one place.

projects.title: Rowad
projects.summary: Rowad is a financial education and entrepreneurship platform designed to help entrepreneurs discover the knowledge, tools, and resources they need throughout their journey.
projects.briefLead: They needed a more organized digital experience that could bring courses, tools, podcasts, documents, events, and other resources into a clearer ecosystem while helping users discover what matters to them.
projects.problemLead: Rowad offered a wide range of valuable entrepreneurial content, but the experience made it difficult to understand where to start and what to explore next.
projects.approachLead: Restructured the information architecture around clearer content categories and user needs.
projects.approachBody:
The central idea was the Journey Guide: a short personalized flow that understands the user's stage and goals, then connects them with relevant courses, tools, podcasts, documents, and other Rowad resources.

The redesigned experience turns Rowad's content ecosystem into a guided journey. The Journey Guide acts as an intelligent starting point, while the rest of the platform provides structured paths for discovering resources, learning content, podcasts, and practical tools.
projects.shippedHeading: From a resource library to a guided journey.
projects.reflectionLead: The biggest opportunity was not adding more content, but making the existing content easier to understand and act on.
projects.reflectionBody: The Journey Guide gives Rowad a way to connect its ecosystem into a clear next step for every user.

constraints.title: Resources were spread across different areas, making discovery feel fragmented.
Users had little guidance based on their business stage or individual needs.
Content existed as separate resources rather than feeling like one connected journey.

decisions.title: Guided Discovery
decisions.body: Users can start from their needs instead of searching through the entire platform.

decisions.title: Personalized Journey
decisions.body: Recommendations adapt to each entrepreneur's stage, goals, and responses.

decisions.title: Connected Ecosystem
decisions.body: Courses, tools, podcasts, and resources work together as one experience.

metrics.label: Personalized onboarding and recommendations.
Structured access to courses, tools, and resources.
A richer way to explore stories and entrepreneurial insights.

seo.metaDescription: Rowad is a financial education and entrepreneurship platform designed to help entrepreneurs discover the knowledge, tools, and resources they need throughout their journey.

projects.title: Lebanese Prime Minister
projects.summary: A redesigned digital home for the Lebanese Prime Minister's Office, bringing government information, legislation, institutional content, and national history into a clearer and more accessible experience.
projects.briefLead: The project focused on restructuring the government portal around clearer information hierarchy, simpler navigation, responsive layouts, and better ways to explore complex institutional, legal, and historical content.
projects.problemLead: The existing website had grown into a large collection of government information, but its structure made important content difficult to understand, scan, and navigate.
projects.approachLead: Restructured the information architecture around user needs and introduced a clearer hierarchy across the platform.
projects.approachBody:
Key experiences were redesigned individually: the Official Gazette around browsing and reading, and the Grand Serail around visual storytelling and chronological exploration.

The redesigned portal creates a clearer path through government information, institutions, legislation, and history. Responsive layouts support different screen sizes, while focused experiences make the Official Gazette easier to explore and transform the Grand Serail into a narrative historical journey.
projects.shippedHeading: A government portal designed around information, not just pages.
projects.reflectionLead: The goal was not simply to make a government website look newer.
projects.reflectionBody: It was to make a complex institutional system easier to understand by giving different types of information the hierarchy, navigation, and interaction patterns they require.

constraints.title: Large volumes of information were presented with weak visual hierarchy.
The navigation structure made it difficult to understand how sections and institutions were connected.
Content-heavy experiences such as the Official Gazette and Grand Serail relied on static presentation instead of discovery and storytelling.

decisions.title: Clearer Navigation
decisions.body: A simplified structure makes government information easier to reach and understand.

decisions.title: Better Reading
decisions.body: The Official Gazette is organized around browsing, filtering, and document access.

decisions.title: Narrative History
decisions.body: The Grand Serail becomes a visual timeline connecting places, moments, and history.

metrics.label: A clearer structure for ministries, institutions, and government information.
A redesigned experience for discovering issues, dates, categories, and documents.
A narrative-driven history experience built around visual moments and chronology.

seo.metaDescription: A redesigned digital home for the Lebanese Prime Minister's Office, bringing government information, legislation and national history into one accessible place.

projects.title: Apamea
projects.summary: Apamea is a multi-asset management platform designed to give investors a clearer view of their wealth by bringing different investment types into one structured workspace.
projects.briefLead: They needed a unified platform for managing different types of assets, replacing fragmented tracking with a structured workspace for monitoring portfolios, positions, performance, and investment activity.
projects.problemLead: Managing different investments often means working across different tools and data structures, making it difficult to maintain a clear picture of overall performance.
projects.approachLead: Designed Apamea around a centralized asset-management model, creating shared interaction patterns across investment types while preserving the information unique to each asset class.
projects.approachBody:
The experience connects high-level portfolio visibility with detailed asset views.

Apamea brings multiple investment categories into one workspace, with dedicated experiences for stocks, real estate, crypto, private equity, and other assets. Consistent navigation, portfolio controls, performance indicators, and detailed views make a complex financial system easier to understand and manage.
projects.reflectionLead: The challenge was not simply presenting more financial data. It was creating a system where different types of investments could feel coherent.
projects.reflectionBody: Apamea connects those experiences through a shared structure while allowing each asset class to surface what matters most.

constraints.title: Different asset classes required different ways of tracking value and performance.
Large amounts of financial data made important information difficult to scan and compare.
Without a unified overview, understanding the bigger portfolio picture became harder.

decisions.title: One Portfolio
decisions.body: A centralized view of assets and investments across different categories.

decisions.title: Deeper Visibility
decisions.body: Detailed views expose valuation, performance, positions, and asset-specific information.

decisions.title: Structured Management
decisions.body: Consistent patterns make a complex multi-asset system easier to operate.

metrics.label: A centralized workspace for switching portfolios and understanding holdings.
Position management, valuation, performance, P/L, and portfolio views.
Project tracking for budgets, margins, stages, and activity.

seo.metaDescription: Apamea is a multi-asset management platform designed to give investors a clearer view of their wealth by bringing different investment types into one structured workspace.

projects.title: MyLebPass
projects.summary: MyLebPass is a digital membership that unlocks offers at restaurants, cafés, and lifestyle venues across Lebanon — one pass, scanned at the counter.
projects.briefLead: They needed a mobile experience that could make a paid membership feel worth it from the first use, turning a list of partner venues into something people open before deciding where to go.
projects.problemLead: A discount pass only works if people remember it exists and can use it without friction at the counter.
projects.approachLead: Designed the pass around the two moments that actually matter: deciding where to go, and redeeming once you are there.
projects.approachBody:
Browsing is organised by venue type and area, so the catalogue reads like somewhere to go tonight rather than a directory to search. Redemption is a single screen holding the member's QR code, reachable in one tap from anywhere in the app.

The value of the membership is kept visible rather than buried in a settings page: what each venue offers, and what the pass has saved so far, sit alongside the browsing experience so the fee keeps justifying itself.
projects.reflectionLead: The hard part of a discount product is not the discount.
projects.reflectionBody: It is being present at the moment someone decides where to go, and effortless at the moment they pay. Both are interface problems more than pricing problems.

constraints.title: Members have to believe a yearly fee will pay for itself before they have used the pass even once.
Redemption happens in public, at a till, with people waiting — it has to take seconds, not menus.
Offers spread across venue types and towns are hard to browse when they are presented as one long list.

decisions.title: Worth It Upfront
decisions.body: Savings are shown against the membership price, so the pass proves its value early instead of asking for faith.

decisions.title: Two-Tap Redemption
decisions.body: The QR code is never more than a tap away, so using the pass at a counter is quicker than explaining it.

decisions.title: Browsable, Not Searchable
decisions.body: Venues are grouped by type and area, so members can choose somewhere without already knowing what they want.

metrics.label: One QR code that works across every partner venue, with no codes to remember.
Partner restaurants, cafés, and lifestyle spots grouped by category and area.
What each venue gives members, and what the pass has saved them so far.

seo.metaDescription: MyLebPass is a digital membership that unlocks offers at restaurants, cafés, and lifestyle venues across Lebanon — one pass, scanned at the counter.

projects.title: Tahweel
projects.summary: A self-initiated redesign of Tahweel, a MENA app for instant gaming top-ups, mobile recharges, gift cards, and eSIMs. Concept work — never handed over or implemented.
projects.briefLead: This one had no client and no brief. I use the product, kept noticing the same friction, and set myself the exercise of reworking it around how quickly someone can finish a task they have already done a dozen times.
projects.briefBody: Nothing here was commissioned by Tahweel, delivered to their team, or shipped. It is a personal study of an app I know well.
projects.problemLead: An app that sells many different digital products drifts towards being a catalogue, when most people open it to repeat one purchase they have made before.
projects.approachLead: Restructured the home screen around repeat purchases instead of around the product catalogue.
projects.approachBody:
The first thing a returning user sees is what they bought last time, one tap from buying it again. Categories still exist, but they are somewhere you go when you want something new, not the toll you pay on every visit.

Checkout was rebuilt around confidence: what is being bought, for which account, at what price, and when it arrives — all visible before the payment step rather than after it.
projects.shippedHeading: A concept, explored end to end.
projects.reflectionLead: Redesigning something nobody asked you to redesign is a good way to find out whether you understand the problem or just dislike the layout.
projects.reflectionBody: The interesting constraint here was restraint: the existing product works, and most of what I changed was hierarchy rather than features. If it were ever built, the next step would be checking the repeat-purchase assumption against real usage data rather than my own habits.

constraints.title: Gaming top-ups, mobile recharges, gift cards, and eSIMs are four different products competing for the same home screen.
Most sessions repeat a previous purchase, but every visit is treated as a first visit.
Paying for digital credit needs visible reassurance at the exact moment of checkout, not in a policy page.

decisions.title: Repeat First
decisions.body: The home screen leads with what this person actually buys, so the common case takes one tap.

decisions.title: One Category at a Time
decisions.body: Four unrelated product types stop competing for attention and get their own focused space.

decisions.title: Trust at Checkout
decisions.body: Account, price, and delivery are confirmed before payment, where the doubt actually happens.

metrics.label: Recent purchases promoted to the top, with categories a step behind.
Focused space for top-ups, recharges, gift cards, and eSIMs.
Account, price, and delivery confirmed before the payment step.

seo.metaDescription: A self-initiated redesign of Tahweel, a MENA app for instant gaming top-ups, mobile recharges, gift cards, and eSIMs. Concept work — never handed over or implemented.

projects.title: RM Luxury
projects.summary: A self-initiated redesign for a private-chauffeur and concierge service, working out how a quote-only offer sells itself with no prices to show. Concept work — never commissioned or built.
projects.briefLead: No client and no brief on this one. Chauffeur and concierge sites kept striking me as the same page every time — a lot of adjectives about discretion and excellence, and almost nothing a visitor can actually decide between — so I set myself the exercise of building one that sells the service without any of that.
projects.briefBody: Nothing here was commissioned by anyone, delivered to a team, or built. It is a personal study of a category I find badly served.
projects.problemLead: A service with no published prices and no availability calendar has nothing concrete to put on a page, which is why so many of them fall back on adjectives.
projects.approachLead: Let the fleet and the occasions do the explaining, and treat the quote as the product rather than as a fallback.
projects.approachBody:
The service picker puts the four offers behind one set of tabs so the site can be broad without the home page having to be. Inside Transport, each vehicle gets the full width and a single specification line — the class and the fact that reservation is on quotation — because those are the two things a visitor is actually deciding between.

The rest is photography doing work the copy cannot. Where a competitor would write about discretion, this shows a driver holding a door, a family arriving at a hotel, a room set for an event. Type stays quiet and black on white so nothing competes with it.
projects.approachCaption: The service picker, with the fleet given the full width of the page.
projects.shippedHeading: The pages that carry the offer.
projects.reflectionLead: Redesigning a category rather than a product means the brief is entirely mine, which makes it easy to solve a problem nobody has.
projects.reflectionBody: The discipline I set myself was to remove a claim every time I wanted to add one, and let the fleet, the occasions, and a very plain type treatment carry the positioning instead. Whether that actually converts better than the adjectives is exactly the thing a self-initiated concept cannot tell you — it would need a real operator, real enquiries, and something to compare against.

constraints.title: Transport, travel, restaurants, and hotels are four unrelated offers coming from one small operation.
Nothing can carry a price, so every route has to end in a quote without that reading as a dead end.
The category is judged on discretion, and a site that tries too hard says the opposite of what it means to.

decisions.title: One Picker, Four Services
decisions.body: Transport, travel, restaurants, and hotels share a single tabbed surface instead of four competing sections.

decisions.title: Quote as the Destination
decisions.body: Every route ends at the same enquiry, stated plainly on the card rather than hidden behind a price nobody can publish.

decisions.title: Photography Over Adjectives
decisions.body: The standard of the service is shown in the images so the copy never has to claim it.

metrics.label: A horizontal set of offers with the enquiry available from the first screen.
The case for the company, split between two calls to action rather than one.
One vehicle at a time, with class and reservation terms stated on the card.

seo.metaDescription: A self-initiated redesign for a private-chauffeur and concierge service, working out how a quote-only offer sells itself with no prices to show.

projects.title: Club Expert+ — Phonak
projects.summary: A membership app for the hearing-care professionals in Phonak's Club Expert+ programme, gathering the news, training, product documents, and priority support they were chasing across other channels.
projects.briefLead: Phonak's partner professionals already had the benefits of the Club Expert+ programme. What they did not have was one place to use them, so the material lived in inboxes, portals, and phone calls.
projects.briefBody: The app had to serve people who open it between patient appointments, on a shop floor, with a few minutes at most — and who are the reason the programme exists rather than its audience of last resort.
projects.problemLead: A membership programme is only worth as much as the speed at which a member can use it, and this one was spread across every channel except a single one.
projects.approachLead: Give each kind of content its own tab, make the documents scannable rather than beautiful, and keep the support line on screen at all times.
projects.approachBody:
The five sections are peers in a bottom bar, so nothing is nested inside anything it does not belong to. Within Products, a second row of tabs separates innovations, range, pricing, and ordering — four questions a professional arrives with already formed, rather than four categories they have to browse.

Document rows state their format and their action before anything else: a PDF badge, a download control, an external-link mark. Someone scanning for the price list should not have to open anything to find out what a row is. The priority call button floats above all of it, because the benefit people joined for should never be somewhere you have to navigate to.

The onboarding does the one job onboarding can honestly do here — naming the three benefits before the member is dropped into a feed that assumes they know what the programme includes.
projects.approachCaption: The news feed, an article, an embedded video, and the empty state.
projects.shippedHeading: The screens a member actually opens.
projects.reflectionLead: Most of this app is a list of documents, and pretending otherwise would have made it worse.
projects.reflectionBody: The useful work was in the rows rather than the flourishes: what a member can tell about a file before tapping it, and how few taps sit between opening the app and reaching the thing they came for. The part I would want to test with real members is the five-way split, which is a reasonable model of the programme but not yet a proven model of their day.

constraints.title: Five unrelated kinds of content — news, training, products, professional tools, communication tools — all belong on the first screen.
Most of the value is PDFs and links, which is the least engaging material an app can be built from.
Priority support is the headline benefit, and burying it two taps deep would undercut the whole proposition.

decisions.title: Five Peers, No Nesting
decisions.body: Each kind of content gets a tab of its own instead of being filed under a section it only half belongs to.

decisions.title: Rows That Declare Themselves
decisions.body: Format and action are visible before the title is read, so a document list can be scanned rather than opened.

decisions.title: Support Always in Reach
decisions.body: The priority line floats over every screen, because it is the benefit the membership is actually sold on.

metrics.label: Three benefits named before the member reaches the feed.
Articles, polls, and video in one feed, with a stated empty state.
Innovations, range, pricing, and ordering split across their own tabs.

projects.title: Archlist
projects.summary: A project-management web app for architects — phases, documents, suppliers, object catalogues and finances — designed inside a visual direction owned by the client, and an exercise in advocating for UX changes within it.
projects.briefLead: Archlist follows an architectural project from first sketch to handover: the phase it is in, the documents that prove it, the trades working on it, and the objects specified along the way.
projects.briefBody: The client arrived with a fully formed visual identity and a clear picture of how the product should look and read. The design work happened inside that picture rather than in place of it.
projects.problemLead: An architectural project has a chronology everybody in the profession knows and almost no software reflects, so the phase you are in has to be read off the documents that exist.
projects.approachLead: Work the improvements into the established direction rather than around it, and make every change one that could be argued for in the client's own terms.
projects.approachBody:
This was the most constrained brief in this portfolio, and the constraint was the interesting part. The identity — the script wordmark, the navy, the topographic ground, the section titles set as watermarks — was not up for discussion, and neither was the overall shape of the product. Colour, typography and the general feel of the thing were the client's own work and they were closely attached to all of it. Proposing a different direction would have been the wrong instinct as well as an unwelcome one.

So the case for each change was made in the client's language and against their own goals: legibility for their clients, fewer places to look, less repeated data entry. That case rarely landed the first time it was made. Most of it was put, reviewed, set aside, and brought back in the next meeting with the reasoning rewritten around something the client had already said they wanted — over a long run of those meetings.

The phase timeline is where the method worked best. It keeps the ornament and the profession's own vocabulary, and adds a state model underneath it — a phase lights up when a document is filed against it, and the furthest lit phase is marked as where the project has reached. The architect gets their chronology; their client gets a progress indicator; nothing about the look had to change to get both. That last clause is why it was accepted.

The same method runs through the rest. The object catalogue carries the fields a specification actually needs — type, sub-type, manufacturer — with the file thumbnails and their overflow count shown on the card, so a card answers a question rather than inviting a click. Inspirations sits next to an image generator, which is the client's idea, given a place in the flow where it supports the moodboard rather than interrupting it.
projects.approachCaption: The phase timeline, with phases lit by the documents filed against them.
projects.shippedHeading: The sections the practice works in.
projects.reflectionLead: The hard part of this project was never a screen. It was making the case for a change again, in the next meeting, after it had already been turned down once.
projects.reflectionBody:
I want to be straight about the outcome, because the process is the part worth showing. A number of the recommendations I believed in most — several of them about colour and about how much visual weight the interface carries — did not survive. They were heard, considered, and shipped the client's way. I kept returning to a few of them across months of reviews, and some of those eventually landed once I found the argument that connected them to something the client already wanted. Others never did.

Working inside a direction somebody else owns and is attached to means every recommendation costs a conversation, and you have to decide which ones are worth spending. That is a real skill and it is not the same skill as being right. The product is better in the places where I did that work patiently, and unchanged in the places where I could not — and a designer who only shows the projects where they had a free hand is not showing you very much about how they work.

constraints.title: The design direction — colour, typography, and the overall feel — was established and owned by the client before the UX work began, and the brief was to develop it rather than to reconsider it.
Every improvement had to be argued on the client’s own terms and survive repeated review, which meant choosing carefully which recommendations were worth the conversation.
Five sections, each dense enough to be its own product, have to sit under one navigation without any of them feeling secondary.
The phase timeline has to be legible to an architect at a glance and to a client who has never seen ESQ, APS, or APD written down.

decisions.title: Phases Lit by Evidence
decisions.body: A phase activates when a document is filed against it, so progress is derived from the work rather than self-reported.

decisions.title: Cards That Answer First
decisions.body: Type, sub-type, manufacturer, and the attachment count are on the card, so browsing a catalogue does not mean opening it.

decisions.title: Change Argued, Not Imposed
decisions.body: Every UX proposal was framed against the client's own stated goals, which is what kept the direction intact and the improvements in it.

metrics.label: The profession's phase chronology, with state driven by filed documents.
Trades, inspirations, objects, and warranties under one set of tabs.
A specification catalogue built to be scanned, with attachments shown on the card.

projects.title: Wise Academy
projects.summary: An admin system for a private school in the US: one place to follow enrolments, search student and parent records, schedule interviews, and send the messages that go with them.
projects.briefLead: They needed a modern, scalable, and user-friendly back-office solution to streamline student enrollment, track records, and manage communication effectively.
projects.problemLead: Wise Academy faced challenges with their existing student management system, which was outdated, unintuitive, and lacked features to handle the increasing number of students.
projects.approachLead: Created low-fidelity wireframes to map out the core functionality, including:
projects.approachBody:
• A dashboard with overview of active and pending enrollments.
• A student database with advanced filters and search functionality.
• A students/parents database with advanced filters and search functionality.
• A calendar tool for managing interviews.

Built interactive prototypes to test key workflows:
• Adding and updating student data.
• Filtering old and new students by batch, grades, or status.
• Managing communication (e.g., sending emails or notifications, interviews).

The final designs were clean, professional, and aligned with Wise Academy's branding. Key features included:
• Dashboard Analytics: Visualized enrollment trends.
• Student Management Module: Easy-to-use interface for adding, editing, and searching student records.
• Automated notification system to remind parents for upcoming payments, deadlines and interviews.
projects.shippedHeading: The screens that carry the work.
projects.reflectionLead: Staff praised the intuitive design and improved workflows.
projects.reflectionBody: Wise Academy expressed interest in extending the platform for managing other aspects of school operations.

constraints.title: Staff struggled with locating and updating student data quickly.
New enrollments required multiple manual steps, leading to delays.
A lack of filtering options for student records made tracking alumni difficult.

decisions.title: Improved Efficiency
decisions.body: Reduced time spent managing student data by 40%.

decisions.title: Streamlined Enrollment
decisions.body: Created a path to view and find student records within seconds.

decisions.title: Enhanced Usability

projects.title: Kabbara Office
projects.summary: Kabbara Office is a digital solution built to help Deputy Karim Kabbara manage and respond to public service requests efficiently.
projects.briefLead: The platform allows users to submit various help requests (legal, financial, employment, etc.) and enables the deputy’s team to track, filter, and manage these cases with clarity and speed.
projects.problemLead: Deputy Karim Kabbara's office faced growing difficulty managing a high volume of public assistance requests using traditional methods.
projects.approachLead: Created low-fidelity wireframes focused on core workflows:
projects.approachBody:
• Services dashboard showing new and pending requests.
• Search and filter functionality to quickly locate requests.
• Request detail view with status updates and user info.

Built interactive prototypes to validate workflows:
• Receiving and tagging new requests by type (legal, financial, etc.).
• Changing request statuses (new, pending, approved, rejected).
• Filtering services by type and requester name.

The final UI reflected an official, clean, and highly readable design. Highlights included:
• A color-coded system for request status.
• Easy-to-use filters and categorization tools.
• Arabic-first design for accessibility to the intended audience.
projects.shippedHeading: The screens that carry the work.
projects.reflectionLead: Deputy's team appreciated the clarity and ease of use.
projects.reflectionBody: The Deputy expressed interest in expanding the system to manage more public-facing initiatives.

constraints.title: Manual request handling was time-consuming and prone to errors.
There was no unified view of pending, approved, or rejected services.
Categorizing and prioritizing new requests lacked a clear workflow.

decisions.title: Centralized Request Management
decisions.body: All requests are now logged and easily trackable in one place.

decisions.title: Clear Status Indicators
decisions.body: Staff can instantly see which requests are new, pending, or completed.

decisions.title: Faster Response Times
decisions.body: Filtering and search tools significantly reduced the time to locate and act on requests.

metrics.label: A colour-coded system for request status across the whole queue.

Designed Arabic-first for accessibility to the intended audience.

projects.title: WFK Law Firm
projects.summary: WFK Law Firm is a professional legal firm that needed an internal tool to streamline employee task tracking, scheduling, and performance monitoring.
projects.briefLead: I was brought in to design a robust task management system and a comprehensive dashboard to centralize daily operations and improve internal accountability — all while ensuring compatibility with Microsoft Power Apps.
projects.problemLead: The firm was using fragmented tools and manual methods to assign, monitor, and manage employee tasks, which led to inefficiencies, miscommunication, and a lack of visibility over day-to-day operations.
projects.approachLead: Created wireframes aligned with Power Apps constraints, focusing on:
projects.approachBody:
• Task creation and assignment flows.
• A calendar-style scheduler for tasks and deadlines.
• A dashboard overview with task status, deadlines, and user performance.

Developed prototypes that allowed stakeholders to:
• Simulate task assignment, editing, and completion flows.
• Navigate a dashboard showing active tasks, overdue actions, and staff activity.
• Filter and sort tasks by status, assignee, or priority.

The final UI design maintained a balance between Power Apps compatibility and clean, functional UX. Key UI aspects included:
• A visually organized task board with clear status indicators.
• A high-contrast layout for easy readability across legal teams.
• Seamless integration feel within Microsoft’s ecosystem.
projects.shippedHeading: The screens that carry the work.
projects.reflectionLead: Both legal staff and managers found the system intuitive and time-saving.
projects.reflectionBody: WFK Law Firm was impressed with how the tool improved internal transparency and organization.

constraints.title: Employees lacked a unified interface to view or manage their assigned tasks.
There was no performance tracking mechanism or analytics overview for management.
The solution needed to align with Power Apps limitations while maintaining good UX practices.

decisions.title: Task Ownership
decisions.body: Employees can now clearly view and manage their assignments in real time.

decisions.title: Executive Overview
decisions.body: The dashboard provides management with performance insights and workload balance.

decisions.title: System Integration
decisions.body: The design was fully Power Apps compatible, ensuring smooth implementation within the existing IT infrastructure.

metrics.label: A visually organised board with clear status indicators.

Designed to sit naturally inside the existing Microsoft ecosystem.

projects.title: Shipment Share
projects.summary: Shipment Share is a smart delivery platform that connects people who need to send packages with travelers already heading to the same destination.
projects.briefLead: I designed the app to streamline the peer-to-peer shipment process, offering an affordable and personal alternative to traditional shipping companies.
projects.briefBody: Users can browse upcoming trips, track shipments, and communicate directly with couriers — all in a clean, mobile-friendly interface.
projects.problemLead: Shipping costs are rising, and traditional courier services can be slow or inaccessible in certain regions.
projects.approachBody:
• Browsing and filtering trips by date and destination.
• Viewing shipment details and sending requests.
• Chat functionality between sender and traveler.

Tested interactive flows with users for:
• Booking a shipment with a traveler.
• Navigating a shipment summary and communication options.
• Viewing shipment status and trip details.

The final UI focused on:
• A bright, intuitive interface using yellow and navy for contrast.
• Minimal steps from finding a trip to booking a shipment.
• A clear shipment breakdown with sender/recipient info, timeline, capacity, and pricing.
projects.shippedHeading: The screens that carry the work.
projects.reflectionLead: Testers praised the clarity of trip details and the ease of contacting travelers.
projects.reflectionBody: Shipment Share’s team appreciated the friendly UI and its appeal to both casual and business users.

constraints.title: Travelers wanted an easy way to offer extra luggage space for delivery without being overwhelmed.
Senders needed to trust the traveler, know the exact route, and have direct communication.
A clear visual summary of the trip, shipment capacity, and fees was essential to both parties.

decisions.title: Real-Time Matchmaking
decisions.body: Travelers and senders can easily connect based on route and availability.

decisions.title: Trust-Driven UI
decisions.body: Clear sender/recipient info, travel timelines, and secure communication features.

decisions.title: Mobile Focus
decisions.body: Designed with mobile-first principles for everyday accessibility and fast interactions.

metrics.label: Browse and filter trips by date and destination, then request a shipment.

projects.title: Shareb
projects.summary: Shareb is a promotional lottery app designed to boost brand engagement through interactive weekly draws.
projects.briefLead: Users can sign up by scanning a QR code printed on branded drink cups and instantly join weekly prize draws with just one tap.
projects.briefBody: The app connects businesses with customers through playful engagement, making every sip a chance to win.
projects.problemLead: Brands needed a fun, cost-effective way to engage customers offline and online, while consumers love winning but are often overwhelmed by complicated sign-up processes.
projects.approachBody:
• Fast sign-up via mobile number and QR scan.
• Clear and fun CTA to 'Join the Draw'.
• Sections for featured brands, prizes, and winner highlights.

Interactive prototypes tested with users to validate the main flow: scan > tap > wait for the draw. Added social buttons and gamified elements to encourage sharing.

The final interface is:
• Bold, playful, and brand-aligned with teal, orange, and animated wheel graphics.
• Designed for repeat visits, with brand carousel and gift previews.
• Light and responsive for instant access after QR scanning.
projects.shippedHeading: The screens that carry the work.
projects.reflectionLead: Users described it as 'super quick' and 'fun to use after grabbing coffee'.
projects.reflectionBody: Shareb’s sponsors praised the exposure and engagement, especially during live campaigns.

constraints.title: QR code scanning had to be seamless and redirect users directly into the app or sign-up screen.
The lottery button needed to feel satisfying and responsive — giving a mini dopamine hit.
Showcasing past winners and brand sponsors built trust and encouraged participation.

decisions.title: Instant Access
decisions.body: Users can enter the draw in seconds with no complicated forms.

decisions.title: Brand-Driven UI
decisions.body: Sponsors and partner logos are clearly featured for visibility.

decisions.title: Gamified Interaction
decisions.body: Tapping to participate adds a game-like layer to simple actions.

metrics.label: Scan the QR code on the cup, tap once, and you are in the draw.
Sponsors and partner logos featured for visibility.
Past winners and prizes shown to build trust and encourage entry.

seo.metaDescription: Shareb is a promotional lottery app designed to boost brand engagement through interactive weekly draws.
